content: Ocular surface burns can result from exposure to chemicals, such as alkalis and acids, or direct thermal injury. These burns can cause significant damage to the limbal epithelial stem cells, leading to delayed re-epithelialization, stem cell failure, and conjunctivalization of the cornea. Amniotic membrane transplantation (AMT), when performed within the acute phase (day 0 to day 7) after such burns, has been proposed as a treatment to alleviate pain and promote healing. The procedure involves attaching a layer of amniotic membrane to the eyelid margins to cover the entire ocular surface. However, there is ongoing debate regarding the severity of burns that might benefit from AMT and whether this intervention improves clinical outcomes. The objective of this study was to compare the effects of AMT combined with medical therapy during the first seven days after an ocular surface burn to medical therapy alone. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and clinical trial registries, was conducted without restrictions on date or language. The last search was performed on September 29, 2021. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated AMT in addition to medical therapy versus medical therapy alone were included. The primary outcomes assessed were failure of re-epithelialization by day 21 post-injury, visual acuity at final follow-up, corneal neovascularization, symblepharon formation, time to re-epithelialization, and adverse effects. Two RCTs were analyzed, with data from patients treated outside the acute phase excluded. A total of 36 cases of moderate burns and 92 cases of severe burns were evaluated separately. The certainty of the evidence was downgraded due to high risks of performance and detection biases, as well as imprecision reflected by wide confidence intervals. Additionally, follow-up intervals were insufficient to accurately determine the time to re-epithelialization. For moderate ocular burns (Roper-Hall classification II-III), the relative risk of AMT on failure of epithelialization by day 21 was 0.18 (95% CI: 0.02 to 1.31), suggesting a potential benefit. LogMAR visual acuity was 0.32 lower (95% CI: 0.55 to 0.09 lower) in the AMT group, indicating better visual outcomes. However, the GRADE assessment for these outcomes was downgraded to very low or low due to bias and imprecision. The effects of AMT on corneal neovascularization (RR 0.56; 95% CI: 0.21 to 1.48), symblepharon formation (RR 0.41; 95% CI: 0.02 to 9.48), and time to re-epithelialization (13 days shorter; 95% CI: 26.30 days shorter to 0.30 days longer) also suggested possible benefits, but the wide confidence intervals indicated uncertainty, with potential for both harm and benefit. Adverse effects were rare, and the small sample size limited the ability to detect rare but significant adverse events. The GRADE assessment for adverse effects was considered low. For severe ocular burns (Roper-Hall classification IV), the relative risk of AMT on failure of epithelialization by day 21 was 1.03 (95% CI: 0.94 to 1.12), and LogMAR visual acuity was 0.01 higher (95% CI: 0.29 lower to 0.31 higher) in the AMT group, indicating no significant benefit. The effects of AMT on corneal neovascularization (RR 0.84; 95% CI: 0.66 to 1.06), symblepharon formation (RR 0.89; 95% CI: 0.56 to 1.42), and time to re-epithelialization (1.66 days shorter; 95% CI: 11.09 days shorter to 7.77 days longer) were similarly inconclusive, with confidence intervals encompassing both harm and benefit. The GRADE assessments for these outcomes were downgraded to low due to bias and imprecision. Adverse effects were again assessed as low-certainty evidence due to the small sample sizes. In conclusion, the evidence supporting the use of AMT in addition to standard medical therapy for moderate acute ocular surface burns is uncertain. While there may be potential benefits in preventing failure of epithelialization by day 21, improving visual outcomes, and reducing corneal neovascularization, symblepharon formation, and time to re-epithelialization, the quality of the evidence is very low. For severe burns, the available evidence does not demonstrate any significant benefit of AMT.
